Rocket.Chat anonymous Livechat visitor bootstrap chained to file-upload access AIExploitation Medium
Detects the full unauthenticated exploit chain: a single source registering an anonymous Livechat visitor (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor), requesting a room (GET /api/v1/livechat/room), then reading files via /file-upload/ within a short window. This is the session-bootstrap primitive the exploit uses to mint a valid rc_token/rc_rid before harvesting arbitrary files. Rationale: Chains the three exact endpoints from the PoC (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor, GET /api/v1/livechat/room, GET /file-upload/) within a 10-minute window keyed on source IP — the minimum footprint of the unauthenticated access-control bypass. Individually noisy, together it is the exploit workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A real anonymous helpdesk visitor who opens Livechat and then downloads a file the agent shared (legitimate, same room)
  • Synthetic monitoring that scripts a Livechat conversation end-to-end
  • Support-widget embedded on a high-traffic page generating many short-lived visitor sessions
  • Rocket.Chat mobile/desktop client polling room + upload endpoints during normal use
  • Pen-test / bug-bounty researcher reproducing the chain on an authorized instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the visitor registration and file reads share one SrcIpAddr and that the /file-upload/ requests carry rc_room_type=l; verify the instance version against the patched list. 2) Contain: block the IP at the proxy/WAF and, if unpatched, disable Livechat or upgrade to the fixed build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP to the enumeration-sweep detection to measure how many files were pulled, and review Content-Disposition/response sizes to identify sensitive filenames leaked.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Url has_any ("/api/v1/livechat/visitor", "/api/v1/livechat/room", "/file-upload/")
| extend isVisitor = Url has "/api/v1/livechat/visitor", isRoom = Url has "/api/v1/livechat/room", isFile = Url has "/file-upload/"
| summarize VisitorReg = countif(isVisitor), RoomReq = countif(isRoom), FileReq = countif(isFile), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where VisitorReg >= 1 and RoomReq >= 1 and FileReq >= 1   // same source bootstraps an anon visitor+room then reads uploads within 10m
| order by FileReq desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/visitor" OR Web.uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/room" OR Web.uri_path="/file-upload/*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval isVisitor=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/visitor",1,0), isRoom=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/room",1,0), isFile=if(like(uri_path,"/file-upload/%"),1,0)
| stats sum(isVisitor) as visitorReg sum(isRoom) as roomReq sum(isFile) as fileReq dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest
| where visitorReg>=1 AND roomReq>=1 AND fileReq>=1
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - fileReq
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/visitor" OR Web.uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/room" OR Web.uri_path="/file-upload/*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval isVisitor=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/visitor",1,0), isRoom=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/room",1,0), isFile=if(like(uri_path,"/file-upload/%"),1,0)
| stats sum(isVisitor) as visitorReg sum(isRoom) as roomReq sum(isFile) as fileReq dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest
| where visitorReg>=1 AND roomReq>=1 AND fileReq>=1
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - fileReq
Rocket.Chat file-upload request carrying Livechat auth params (IDOR signature) AIExploitation Medium
Single-event signature for the Rocket.Chat access-control bypass: a GET to /file-upload/ whose query string carries rc_room_type=l together with rc_token — the Livechat authorization path being used to read a file, exactly as in the disclosed exploit. Surfaces individual exploit attempts even below the harvest threshold. Rationale: Uses the verbatim exploit primitive from the PoC — /file-upload/ path plus rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — as an atomic, Sigma-portable signature. It matches even a single probe, complementing the volume- and chain-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Livechat visitor downloading an attachment shared in their own helpdesk room (identical request shape)
  • Rocket.Chat client appending rc_room_type/rc_token to file URLs during normal Livechat file rendering
  • WAF or SSL-inspection proxy replaying the request as part of active response testing
  • Authorized researcher/DAST scan on a staging instance
  • URL-preview/link-unfurl bot following a Livechat file link
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — HTTP 200 means a file was served; note the SrcIpAddr, Content-Disposition filename, and whether the source ever authenticated. 2) Contain: if the instance is unpatched (pre 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13), upgrade or disable Livechat and block the IP. 3) Hunt: aggregate this IP's requests to see if it escalates into the distinct-fileId harvest sweep, and correlate with anonymous visitor registrations from the same address.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and Url has "rc_room_type=l" and Url has "rc_token="
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Twig SSTI markers in request-controlled fields against Craft/Formie public forms AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests carrying Twig template syntax ({{ }}, {% %}) in the User-Agent, Referer, or query string reaching a Craft CMS site running Formie. CVE-2026-52889 copies these request-derived Hidden-field defaults straight into Craft's Twig render layer, so Twig markers in these fields are the earliest observable of exploitation of a public form. Rationale: Uses the exact request-derived input surface named in the advisory (User Agent, Referer, Current URL, Query Parameter) and Twig delimiters {{ / {% (plus URL-encoded %7b%7b). Web-request telemetry only exists in Sentinel W3CIISLog / Splunk Web DM; Defender AH, Datadog standard sources, Falcon FDR and CloudWatch do not carry HTTP request headers, so those queries are intentionally empty. Cross-checked against the sibling Formie SSTI advisory CVE-2026-45697 and the Craft SSTI advisory GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-formie-plugin-twig-injection-via-hidden-field-cve-2026-45697-critical/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web vulnerability scanners (Burp, Nuclei, Acunetix) sending {{7*7}} SSTI probes
  • Client-side JS frameworks (AngularJS/Vue/Mustache) passing {{ }} template strings in query params
  • Marketing/analytics referrers containing mustache placeholders like {{campaign}}
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the public form
  • URLs carrying JSON blobs with doubled braces
Suppression filter
| where scStatus == 200 and csUriStem !contains "/api/" and csUserAgent !has_any ("AngularJS","Vue")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP in the window; confirm the target csUriStem is a page that renders a Formie form and whether scStatus==200 (server processed the payload vs 404/403). Decode the payload from UA/query/cookie. 2) Contain: if the payload contains RCE gadgets or scStatus 200 on a form page, block the source IP at the WAF and confirm Formie is on 3.1.27+; if not, apply the workaround (remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults) immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint telemetry on the web host for php/w3wp spawning shells (UC3) and review the same source IP for gadget strings (UC2).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem !endswith ".js" and csUriStem !endswith ".css" and csUriStem !endswith ".png" and csUriStem !endswith ".woff2"
| where csUriQuery contains "%7b%7b" or csUriQuery contains "{{" or csUriQuery contains "%7b%25" or csUriQuery contains "{%"
     or csUserAgent contains "{{" or csUserAgent contains "{%" or csUserAgent contains "_self.env"
     or csReferer contains "{{" or csReferer contains "{%"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Active Twig RCE gadget strings in Craft/Formie HTTP request inputs AIExploitation High
High-fidelity detection for Twig-to-PHP RCE gadgets (_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback / getFilter / craft.app) delivered via the request-controlled Hidden-field defaults exploited by CVE-2026-52889. Unlike generic {{ }} probing, these tokens are unambiguous command-execution attempts. Rationale: Anchors on the documented Twig RCE gadget chain _self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback + getFilter and Craft's exposed craft.app object — these strings virtually never appear in benign traffic, so this warrants alerting. Web-request headers/query are only available in Sentinel/Splunk web logs; Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch do not carry them. Gadget syntax corroborated via PayloadsAllTheThings PHP SSTI and the Craft SSTI advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://swisskyrepo.github.io/PayloadsAllTheThings/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/PHP/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest/red-team validating CVE-2026-52889 post-patch
  • Vulnerability scanner with a Twig-specific SSTI plugin
  • WAF that replays blocked payloads into a downstream access log
  • Security-training or CTF traffic against a staging Craft instance
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ip_placeholder_removed>") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Nuclei","nuclei","Burp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the full payload from csUriQuery/csUserAgent/csReferer, identify the command inside getFilter()/filter('system'), and check scStatus + the response size for signs the command executed. Confirm the source IP is not an authorized scanner. 2) Contain: block the source IP, take the affected web node out of the pool if RCE is likely, and force-upgrade Formie to 3.1.27+ (or remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults). 3) Hunt: on the web host, run UC3 for php/w3wp child shells, review new files in web roots (webshell drop) and outbound connections from the PHP worker, and search all web logs for the same source IP and gadget tokens over a wider window.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriQuery has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","registerUndefinedFunctionCallback","getFilter","_self.env","craft.app")
     or csUserAgent has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","registerUndefinedFunctionCallback","getFilter","_self.env","craft.app")
     or csReferer has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","getFilter","_self.env")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Craft/PHP/IIS web worker spawning a command shell (Formie SSTI RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the PHP FastCGI, php-fpm, or IIS worker process backing a Craft CMS site spawning a command interpreter or recon LOLBin — the post-exploitation footprint of a successful Twig SSTI RCE via CVE-2026-52889. A web worker launching cmd/powershell/sh is not normal Craft behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the specific web-tier parents of a Craft/PHP deployment (php-cgi.exe, php-fpm, w3wp.exe backing IIS+FastCGI, nginx/httpd) spawning shells/recon LOLBins — the concrete execution outcome of the Twig system()/exec gadget the advisory warns can lead to RCE. Purely endpoint telemetry, so no web-log or CloudWatch query. Not covered by generic Office-spawn-script or encoded-PS rules. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running Craft console commands (php craft resave/queue/run) that legitimately shell out
  • Image-processing plugins (ImageMagick/GD) invoked by php calling system utilities
  • Deployment/build steps (composer, npm) executed under the web-service account
  • Monitoring/backup agents launched by the web worker
  • Scheduled Craft queue jobs spawning curl for outbound webhooks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "craft" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("queue/run","resave","gc","migrate")) and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a shell running whoami/id/net/certutil under the web-service account with no interactive admin session is high-signal; correlate the timestamp with UC1/UC2 web-log hits from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, kill the child process, and revoke/rotate any credentials accessible to the web-service account; confirm Formie is patched to 3.1.27+. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the php/w3wp worker (webshells), outbound connections from the worker process, new local accounts or scheduled tasks, and repeat the process-tree hunt across all other Craft/Formie web nodes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Forged unsigned (alg:none) JWT Bearer token reaching Apache Camel route (CVE-2026-53913) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests whose Authorization: Bearer value is an unsigned/forged JWT — a header decoding to {"alg":"none"} or a token with an empty signature segment — which the vulnerable camel-keycloak KeycloakSecurityPolicy accepts without verification in its default (empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions) config. A forged token that returns HTTP 2xx indicates a successful unauthenticated bypass into server-side route work, up to unauthenticated RCE where the route forwards to a code-execution producer. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete forged-token shape: an unsigned JWT carries a {"alg":"none"} header whose base64url form starts eyJhbGciOiJub25l (alg-first) / eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJub25l (typ-first), and an unsigned JWT has an empty third (signature) segment — both are effectively never produced by a legitimate Keycloak-issued token. Corroborated by IONIX and basefortify write-ups confirming the alg:none/forged-JWT bypass shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-53913/ • https://basefortify.eu/cve_reports/2026/07/cve-2026-53913.html • https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/299985
ATT&CKT1190 T1606
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / pen-test tools (Burp, Nuclei CVE-2026-53913 template, OWASP ZAP) deliberately sending alg:none tokens during an authorized assessment
  • Internal API compatibility tests that intentionally send malformed bearer tokens to validate rejection behaviour
  • A custom identity provider that legitimately issues unsigned tokens over a trusted internal channel (rare, misconfiguration)
  • Copy-paste/truncated tokens in a client bug that drop the signature segment, producing a trailing-dot token
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode >= 200 and HttpStatusCode < 400  // keep only requests the failing-open policy actually let through
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0")  // add authorized scanner source IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the matching requests and check HttpStatusCode — a 2xx/3xx on a route behind KeycloakSecurityPolicy means the bypass succeeded; base64url-decode the Token header to confirm alg:none. Identify the target Camel route and what producer it forwards to (file, exec, http, sql). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, and apply the vendor mitigation now — set a non-empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions on every KeycloakSecurityPolicy (forces the verification path), set allowTokenFromHeader=false where not needed, or add upstream token validation; plan upgrade to camel-keycloak 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. 3) Hunt: review all requests from the same src IP/UA for follow-on actions on the reached route (command execution, file writes, data reads) and pivot to server process/file telemetry on the Camel host for that time window.
// Requires WAF / API-gateway / reverse-proxy logs that capture the Authorization header into ASIM ImWebSession
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| extend AuthHdr = tostring(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where AuthHdr startswith "Bearer " or AuthHdr startswith "bearer "
| extend Token = trim(" ", substring(AuthHdr, 7))
// forged unsigned JWT: base64url of {"alg":"none"...} (alg-first or typ-first), or a JWT with an empty signature segment
| where Token has_any ("eyJhbGciOiJub25l", "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJub25l")
    or Token matches regex @"^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.$"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Token
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable camel-keycloak version exposed (CVE-2026-53913 affected range) AIReconnaissance High
Inventories hosts running Apache Camel camel-keycloak in the vulnerable ranges (>=4.15.0 <4.18.3 and >=4.19.0 <4.21.0) so the SOC can prioritise patching and apply the KeycloakSecurityPolicy mitigation before the auth bypass is exploited. This is an exposure/attack-surface pivot rather than an in-progress-attack detection. Rationale: Directly keys on the article's CVE id (CVE-2026-53913) and the concrete affected package (org.apache.camel:camel-keycloak) and fixed versions 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. Software-inventory match is deterministic, hence high confidence and low FP. Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion falls in >=4.15.0 <4.18.3 or >=4.19.0 <4.21.0, and determine whether the host is internet-facing and whether any route actually uses KeycloakSecurityPolicy with the default empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions. 2) Contain: for exposed vulnerable hosts, apply the interim mitigation immediately (non-empty requiredRoles/requiredPermissions, allowTokenFromHeader=false, or upstream token validation) and schedule upgrade to 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. 3) Hunt: on each confirmed-vulnerable host, run the forged-alg:none-JWT web-log detection over the last 30 days to check for prior exploitation, and review the Camel route configs for producers capable of code execution.

Apache Camel DNS SSRF: inbound HTTP request carrying dns.server / dns.name control headers AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a Camel platform-http endpoint that smuggle the raw dns.server, dns.name, dns.domain, dns.type or dns.class parameters (CVE-2026-48205). Because these names lack the Camel/camel prefix, HttpHeaderFilterStrategy lets them pass from the HTTP boundary into the Exchange, letting an unauthenticated client repoint the DNS resolver or resolve arbitrary internal hostnames. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable parameter names (dns.server / dns.name / dns.domain / dns.type / dns.class) which are the raw pre-fix header/param constants — the migration guidance renames them to CamelDns*, so any surviving dns.* on the HTTP boundary is either an attacker or a pre-upgrade misconfig. Camel platform-http binds both query params and headers into the Exchange, so query-string capture in web logs is a valid vector. Cross-checked GHSA-hcm8-x79p-wx2w and Akamai's Camel header-smuggling write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hcm8-x79p-wx2w • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/march-apache-camel-vulnerability-detections-and-mitigations • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-48205
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Burp/Nuclei) probing the Camel endpoint with dns.* payloads
  • Internal QA/dev traffic still using legacy dns.* header names before completing the CamelDns* migration
  • A legitimately-designed DNS-lookup API that intentionally exposes a dns.name / dns.domain query parameter
  • Synthetic monitoring/health-check tooling replaying old request templates
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei" and RequestClientApplication !has "Burp" | where SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external/untrusted and check the HTTP response status — a 200 with the app reaching the camel-dns producer indicates successful exploitation; note the dns.server value (attacker resolver) and any dns.name/dns.domain values (internal hosts probed). 2) Contain: add a WAF rule to strip/deny dns.server, dns.name, dns.domain, dns.type, dns.class and term on ingress, and prioritise upgrading Camel to 4.14.8 / 4.18.3 / 4.21.0. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound DNS from the app host (UC2) to spot the SSRF egress, and search the same logs for other prefix-less Camel header smuggling and for internal hostnames enumerated via dns.name/dns.domain.

| where RequestURL has_any ("dns.server","dns.name","dns.domain","dns.type","dns.class")
    or RequestContext has_any ("dns.server","dns.name","dns.domain","dns.type","dns.class")
    or Message has_any ("dns.server","dns.name","dns.domain","dns.type","dns.class")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Apache Camel DNS SSRF egress: app server (java) resolving via external / attacker DNS resolver AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the server-side effect of CVE-2026-48205: the Camel JVM issuing DNS queries (UDP/53) to a public resolver it should never talk to, because an attacker set dns.server to point SimpleResolver at an attacker-controlled DNS server. Internal app servers normally resolve only via internal forwarders, so outbound port-53 to a public IP from java is high-signal SSRF egress. Rationale: Targets the concrete SSRF payoff described in the advisory — SimpleResolver pointed at an attacker DNS server — by flagging java issuing UDP/53 to any non-private, non-corporate resolver, which is anomalous for a backend app that should use internal forwarders. Corporate public resolvers are allow-listed to cut noise. Pairs with UC1 (ingress) to confirm end-to-end exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hcm8-x79p-wx2w • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/march-apache-camel-vulnerability-detections-and-mitigations
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Camel route legitimately configured to query a public DNS resolver for a real DNS-integration use case
  • Java-based monitoring/APM agents performing external DNS lookups
  • App server placed in a segment without an internal DNS forwarder, resolving directly to public roots
  • Container images shipping with a hard-coded public resolver (e.g. 8.8.8.8) in resolv.conf overriding corporate DNS
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","9.9.9.9","208.67.222.222","208.67.220.220")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the DstIpAddr/RemoteIP the JVM queried — is it a known corporate/public resolver or an unfamiliar host? Correlate the same host+time window against UC1 web logs for an inbound dns.server=<that IP> request to confirm attacker control. 2) Contain: block egress UDP/53 from the app subnet to anything but internal forwarders, and repoint the Camel DNS server parameter to a trusted source in the route (or upgrade to 4.21.0/4.18.3/4.14.8). 3) Hunt: enumerate the dns.name/dns.domain values queried to see which internal hostnames the attacker probed, and review whether poisoned DNS responses drove any downstream connections from the host.

| where RemoteIP !in ("8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","9.9.9.9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName

phpBB CVE-2026-48611 auth bypass via login_link auth_provider=apache AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact CVE-2026-48611 exploit request: a single unauthenticated POST to ucp.php that triggers the login-link flow but forces the vulnerable 'apache' auth provider (auth_provider=apache) to skip the password check and log in as any user. The auth_provider=apache value inside a mode=login_link request is a near-unambiguous exploit signature that no legitimate default phpBB flow produces. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim PoC URL (/ucp.php?mode=login_link&auth_provider=apache&login_link_aikido=1); auth_provider=apache in a login_link request is the exact exploit primitive and has no benign default-config equivalent. Cross-checked against Pentest-Tools, IONIX, SentinelOne, phpBB.com advisory and public PoC repos. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-48611/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48611/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanning (Nuclei has a public CVE-2026-48611 template) hitting the endpoint
  • Internal penetration-test / red-team validation of the patch
  • A phpBB instance legitimately fronted by an Apache .htpasswd proxy that genuinely uses the apache auth provider (rare, non-default)
  • Security researchers reproducing the PoC from the aikido.dev / GitHub repos against a lab instance
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<scanner-ip-allowlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target forum version — if < 3.3.17 (or 4.0.0-a2) it is exploitable; capture source IP, User-Agent, targeted login_username, and the HTTP status (302 = successful bypass). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, force-expire all active phpBB sessions (rotate the board's session salt / clear phpbb_sessions), and prioritise upgrade to 3.3.17 or apply the vendor workaround disabling the apache provider. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same source IP for follow-on /adm/index.php access, ACP user/permission changes, and private-message reads; review phpbb_log for admin actions after the exploit timestamp.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "ucp.php"
| where Url has "mode=login_link" and Url has "auth_provider=apache"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

phpBB CVE-2026-48611 post-exploit ACP access from exploiting IP AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the CVE-2026-48611 exploit request (login_link + auth_provider=apache) with a subsequent hit to the phpBB Admin Control Panel (/adm/index.php) from the same source IP within one hour. This confirms the bypass yielded an admin session and the attacker is now operating the forum backend, separating real compromise from opportunistic scanning. Rationale: Uses the article's ACP path (/adm/index.php) plus the exact exploit query string, tied on source IP within a 1h window (3600s / 1h) — the exploit-then-admin sequence is what turns a scan into confirmed admin takeover. ACP path and admin impact confirmed against phpBB.com advisory and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170 • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass
ATT&CKT1078 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate admin who happens to share a NAT/egress IP with a scanner that probed the endpoint
  • Penetration test that both exploits and logs into ACP from the same host (expected TP but authorized)
  • WAF/proxy that rewrites source IP to a single upstream address, collapsing distinct users onto one src (tune to use X-Forwarded-For)
  • Load-balancer health checks hitting /adm/index.php returning 401/403 (filter on HttpStatusCode success)
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode in (200, 302, 301)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm both events share the true client IP (check XFF if behind a proxy) and that the /adm access returned 200/302 rather than 401/403; identify which admin username was impersonated. 2) Contain: invalidate all sessions, disable/rotate the compromised admin account credentials, block the source IP, and enable maintenance mode until 3.3.17 is deployed. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ACP action from that session — new admin/mod accounts (acp_users, acp_groups), permission grants, board settings and email-config changes, and extension installs (potential webshell); diff phpbb_config and phpbb_users against a known-good backup.
let Exploit = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "ucp.php" and Url has "mode=login_link" and Url has "auth_provider=apache"
    | project ExploitTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname;
ImWebSession

| join kind=inner Exploit on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ExploitTime .. ExploitTime + 1h)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ExploitTime)
| project ExploitTime, AdminAccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode, DelaySec
| order by ExploitTime desc

HTTP Basic Authorization header sent to phpBB login_link endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the mechanism CVE-2026-48611 abuses: an HTTP 'Authorization: Basic' header supplied to phpBB's ucp.php login_link flow, which the apache provider trusts as PHP_AUTH_USER to skip password validation. Default phpBB never uses HTTP Basic authentication, so a Basic header on a login_link request is a strong exploit indicator that survives WAF logs even when query strings are truncated or the provider value varies. Rationale: Anchored on the PoC's 'Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46eA==' header combined with mode=login_link on ucp.php — the apache provider reads PHP_AUTH_USER from exactly this header. Basic auth on phpBB is anomalous by design; the Splunk fallback keys on the login_link POST since CIM Web has no request-header field (the header check requires ImWebSession/WAF telemetry, noted for the analyst). Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/authentication-bypass-phpbb-technical-writeup • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-48611/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A phpBB instance genuinely deployed behind an Apache .htpasswd proxy using the apache auth provider (non-default, legitimate Basic auth)
  • Automated vulnerability scanners replaying the PoC request
  • Browser/basic-auth prompts on a reverse proxy protecting the whole forum with site-wide Basic auth
  • API clients or monitoring tools mistakenly configured to send Basic credentials to ucp.php
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode in (200, 302)
Response runbook
1) Triage: base64-decode the Authorization header to recover the targeted username and check whether the response was a 302 (successful bypass); confirm the forum is not intentionally behind an Apache .htpasswd proxy. 2) Contain: block the source IP, expire active sessions, and fast-track the 3.3.17 upgrade or apply the vendor workaround disabling the apache provider. 3) Hunt: correlate the same IP/username to subsequent /adm/index.php access, private-message reads, and ACP configuration or account changes; review other endpoints for reuse of the same Basic header.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "ucp.php" and Url has "mode=login_link"
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) and HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization startswith "Basic "
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN

          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-02 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A look inside the reverse-engineering journey of building the first RDP client outside of Windows to support WebAuthn redirection. The post How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a self-hosted CI/CD runner process (Runner.Worker/node/python/curl) reaching gist.githubusercontent.com — the exact egress the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action used to pull its memory-dumping Python second stage. This was StepSecurity Harden-Runner's original detection signal for the March 2025 incident. Rationale: Uses the corroborated network IOC (outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com from a runner) that StepSecurity's Harden-Runner used to detect CVE-2025-30066; scoped to runner process ancestry (Runner.Worker/node/python/_actions paths) to separate it from ordinary developer gist fetches. Cross-checked against CISA, Wiz and Sysdig write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build step legitimately curls a config/install script hosted on a GitHub gist
  • Developer tooling or dotfiles bootstrap that pulls from gist.githubusercontent.com on a self-hosted runner
  • Package post-install hooks fetching helper scripts from a gist
  • Security tooling / EDR test harness deliberately reaching gist domains
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation resolving raw gist content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("renovate","dependabot") or RemoteUrl has "raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent chain of the initiating process; confirm it ran inside a GitHub Actions job (Runner.Worker/_work/_actions path) and identify the workflow/repo. Grab the exact gist URL and the resolved IP. 2) Contain: if the job used tj-actions/changed-files (or any action pinned to a mutable tag), pause the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to workflows that ran between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC (access keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, RSA keys). 3) Hunt: search the same runner fleet for the malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 and for double-base64 blobs written to workflow logs; review runner egress for other first-seen domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or RemoteUrl has "gist.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","python3","python","curl.exe","curl","wget","Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker","node.exe","node")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("actions-runner","_work","_actions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or HttpHostName in~ ("gist.githubusercontent.com","gist.github.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066) AIDelivery High
Alerts on the exact malicious tj-actions/changed-files commit SHA (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67) appearing in any process command line or file path on a self-hosted runner — i.e. the compromised action being fetched, checked out, or pinned. A pure, second-source-confirmed IOC hunt for the retagged supply-chain payload. Rationale: Uses the article's SHA1 (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67), independently confirmed by CISA and the GitHub Advisory as the single malicious commit every tj-actions/changed-files tag (v1.0.0–v44.5.1) was pointed to — a unique, zero-ambiguity IOC that only appears when the compromised action is fetched, checked out, or SHA-pinned. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel tooling scanning for the hash as an IOC (grep, EDR IOC sweep) surfaces the string in its own command line
  • A remediation script that greps repos/workflows for the malicious SHA
  • Vulnerability-management agent enumerating the commit as data
  • A security researcher reproducing/analyzing the incident in a lab runner
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","select-string") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC","threat-intel","scan-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA appears in a real action fetch/checkout (Runner.Worker/git/_actions context) versus an analyst's own IOC-scan process; identify the repo and the workflow run time. 2) Contain: treat the runner and any workflow that executed the action as compromised — rotate all secrets exposed to workflows run between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC, and repin tj-actions/changed-files to the patched v46.0.1 by full SHA. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound gist.githubusercontent.com egress from the same runner, inspect workflow logs for double-base64 secret blobs, and check for the sibling reviewdog/action-setup CVE-2025-30154 across the fleet.
let ioc = "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67";
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ioc or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ioc
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", Account=AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where FolderPath has ioc or FileName has ioc or FolderPath has "tj-actions/changed-files"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", Account=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=FolderPath, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner spawns network tool / interpreter under compromised trivy-action or KICS · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TeamPCP Trivy/KICS supply-chain credential exfil to scan.aquasecurtiy.org & 45.148.10.212 · [LLM] DNS resolution of TeamPCP typosquat exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Credential harvest via /proc/<pid>/mem read of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker
TeamPCP Trivy/KICS supply-chain credential exfil to scan.aquasecurtiy.org & 45.148.10.212 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from CI/CD runners (or any onboarded host) to the exact exfiltration infrastructure used by TeamPCP's compromised aquasecurity/trivy-action and Checkmarx KICS actions. Any egress to these hard IOCs means the credential stealer's POST reached the wire. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim exfil host scan.aquasecurtiy.org (typosquat resolving to 45.148.10.212) plus the pre-extracted secondary IOC IPs/domains; connection to any is near-zero-FP and confirms secrets left the runner.
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher deliberately detonating the compromised action in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving/probing the IOC domains
  • A blocked/failed connection logged by a proxy that never actually exfiltrated
  • Internal typosquat-monitoring service crawling lookalike domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/runner and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; confirm whether it is a CI runner that recently executed aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, rotate ALL secrets/tokens exposed to that job (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud OIDC creds, registry creds) and revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: pull every repo/workflow that referenced the compromised action across the org, pivot on the /proc/pid/mem credential-harvest UC, and block the IOC IPs/domains at egress.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43")
   or Url has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcAction, NetworkBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Credential harvest via /proc/<pid>/mem read of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core TeamPCP payload behaviour: a spawned interpreter (python/node/sh) reading /proc/<pid>/mem of the Runner.Worker process to scrape marked secrets from runner memory. This is the article's exact credential-access primitive, independent of the exfil endpoint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact TTP — a payload process reading /proc/pid/mem of the Runner.Worker process — as the pivot; the Runner.Worker parent + interpreter + /proc/*/mem triad is specific to CI runner memory-scraping and rarely legitimate.
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate profiling/debugging tools (gdb, py-spy) attached to a runner job by a maintainer
  • Crash-dump or coredump collection tooling reading /proc during a CI failure
  • Custom self-hosted-runner health scripts inspecting worker memory usage
  • Security agents themselves reading /proc for telemetry
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","gdb","coredumpctl","/usr/bin/perf"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the target PID; confirm the parent is the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker and the child interpreter is not part of the declared workflow. 2) Contain: kill the job, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret injected into that workflow run plus any downstream cloud OIDC tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to the C2 egress UC (scan.aquasecurtiy.org/45.148.10.212) within the same job window, and enumerate all repos referencing aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS by tag.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker" or ProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker"
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3","node","sh","bash","perl","ruby")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ProcessCommandLine has "mem"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","sh","bash","perl","ruby")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "mem"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner.Worker Memory Scrape via /proc/pid/mem
id: c1d4e7a2-5b62-4f18-8a90-77e3b1c2f6d0
description: Detects an interpreter spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process reading /proc/<pid>/mem to extract secrets from runner memory, matching TeamPCP's trivy-action credential stealer.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/10-layers-deep-how-stepsecurity-stops-teampcps-trivy-supply-chain-attack-on-github-actions

logsource:

detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains: 'Runner.Worker'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/proc/'
      - 'mem'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(python OR python3 OR node OR bash OR sh OR perl OR ruby) (@process.command_line:*"/proc/"* AND @process.command_line:*mem*)

| ParentBaseFileName=/Runner\.Worker/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(python3?|node|bash|sh|perl|ruby)$/i
| regex("/proc/", field=CommandLine)
| regex("mem", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
